exercises.prompt: What is the time complexity of this matrix-multiplication routine, as a function of $n$ (the dimension of the two $n \times n$ matrices)?
exercises.explanation: Three nested loops each running $n$ times give $n \times n \times n = n^3$ total iterations — the standard cost of naive matrix multiplication.

exercises.prompt: What is the time complexity of `is_prime` below, as a function of $n$?
exercises.explanation: The loop only needs to check divisors up to $\sqrt{n}$, since any factor larger than that would have a matching factor smaller than $\sqrt{n}$ — so `i` runs from 2 to roughly $\sqrt{n}$.

exercises.prompt: This function is meant to report the full size, in bytes, of the 10-element array passed to it. Why doesn't it work as intended?
choices: It prints 40, exactly as expected — there is no bug
When passed as a function parameter, `arr` decays to a pointer, so `sizeof(arr)` measures the pointer's size, not the array's
`%zu` is the wrong format specifier and the program fails to compile
`sizeof` cannot legally be used inside a function body in C
exercises.answer: When passed as a function parameter, `arr` decays to a pointer, so `sizeof(arr)` measures the pointer's size, not the array's
exercises.explanation: A function parameter declared as `int arr[]` is really `int *arr` — array parameters always decay to a pointer. Inside `printSize`, `sizeof(arr)` is the size of that pointer (commonly 8 bytes), not the 40 bytes of the caller's actual array.

exercises.prompt: This function is meant to check whether two arrays hold the same items, but `hasSameItems([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])` prints `false`. What's the bug?
choices: `===` compares array references, not contents — two distinct arrays are never `===`, even with identical elements
JavaScript can't compare numbers inside arrays
`console.log` silently converts the result to a string first
The function should compare `a.length` instead of `a` and `b`
exercises.answer: `===` compares array references, not contents — two distinct arrays are never `===`, even with identical elements
exercises.explanation: Arrays (and objects) are reference types: `===` checks whether both sides point to the exact same object in memory, not whether their contents match. Comparing contents requires something like element-by-element comparison or `JSON.stringify`.
`a = b = []` binds both names to the same list object, not two separate empty lists. Mutating it through `a` is visible through `b` too.
